speaker: Eric Jang
title: What rebuilding AlphaGo teaches us about self-play, RL, and future of LLMs - Eric Jang
question: In reinforcement learning with tree search, why can training on an off-policy replay buffer help a policy instead of hurting it?
guest: This gets into the fundamental on-policy versus off-policy reinforcement learning question. In MCTS, you take actions you previously took and relabel them to take better actions on the same states. The off-policy issue arises when you are relabeling states that your new policy would never visit. You are wasting capacity, and in the extreme limit, if your training buffer consists entirely of states you would never visit, you are supervising the model to take good actions on states you would never reach, so your policy can get really bad. That is where off-policy data can really hurt. However, if you interpret this from the DAgger perspective—as a way to correct yourself back to the optimal trajectory—what you want is mostly states that your policy would visit, plus a modest percentage of states in a high-dimensional tube around your optimal trajectories. Each of those nearby states is given a supervision target to funnel you back into your optimal trajectory.

points.core: Off-policy buffers hurt when filled with states the policy never visits.
points.note: Accept: supervising unreachable or out-of-distribution states wastes model capacity and degrades the policy. Do not credit: generic warnings that off-policy RL is unstable without citing unreachable state distributions.

points.core: Keeping nearby off-optimal states around the main trajectory builds error recovery.
points.note: Accept: retaining a modest share of states in a tube or neighborhood around optimal trajectories, analogous to DAgger. Do not credit: generic praise for exploration or data diversity without referencing near-trajectory drift states.

points.core: Relabeling drifted states with improved actions funnels the agent back on-track.
points.note: Accept: supervising off-trajectory states with search-relabelled or corrective targets teaches the policy to return to optimal paths. Do not credit: simply saying replay buffers reuse past data without corrective relabeling.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
In AlphaZero/MuZero-style methods, the replay buffer doesn't hurt because the policy isn't trained to imitate the stale actions that older networks happened to take. It is trained toward the search's output: the visit-count distribution MCTS produced at each stored state. Search acts as a policy improvement operator, so those targets are generally better than the raw network policy that generated them, and often still better than the current network's prior. Learning from them is supervised distillation of an improved policy, not an off-policy policy-gradient update, so no importance-sampling correction is needed and the mismatch between behaviour and current policy matters much less.

The buffer also helps in ordinary ways: it decorrelates samples, reuses expensive search results many times, and covers a broader range of states, which stabilises training and reduces forgetting.

Staleness is not free, though. Old search policies and especially value targets (game outcomes or n-step returns under older play) can lag behind the current agent. MuZero Reanalyze addresses this by re-running search with the latest network on stored states, which refreshes the targets and turns old data into new improvement signal.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: In standard policy-gradient learning, training on an off-policy replay buffer can hurt a policy because older trajectories reflect outdated or exploratory behavior, introducing bias and distribution shift. Tree search changes this dynamic because the policy learns by distilling local search targets rather than reinforcing raw past actions. At any state, tree search acts as a local policy-improvement operator: through lookahead and value backups, it computes an action distribution stronger than the behavior network, and buffered states can even be re-searched with the latest model (as in MuZero Reanalyze) to eliminate target staleness. Because supervision depends on planning from a state rather than how the agent arrived there, off-policy states remain valid training inputs. Sampling them from a replay buffer then actively strengthens the policy by amortizing expensive search across multiple updates, decorrelating sequential transitions for stable optimization, and preserving broad state coverage—preventing catastrophic forgetting, self-play cycling, and brittle play outside narrow on-policy trajectories.

noweb.answer: In tree-search reinforcement learning such as AlphaZero, an off-policy replay buffer helps rather than hurts because the policy is trained via supervised distillation of search-improved targets rather than raw on-policy gradients. Standard policy-gradient methods struggle with stale data because past returns reflect an outdated behavior policy, introducing severe bias. With tree search, however, each stored state is paired with a visit distribution refined by multi-step lookahead—a local policy-improvement target that remains informative across recent iterations and can even be recomputed with newer networks, as in MuZero Reanalyze. Because updates minimize state-conditional cross-entropy rather than trajectory-weighted policy gradients, off-policy state distributions do not destabilize optimization. Instead, the buffer actively strengthens the policy: reusing computationally expensive search targets boosts sample efficiency and decorrelates minibatches, preventing overfitting to the latest self-play games. Retaining diverse states from earlier policies also prevents catastrophic forgetting, dampens cyclic self-play dynamics, and keeps the policy prior accurate on suboptimal, off-path branches that future tree searches must still evaluate.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Off-policy data usually hurts plain policy-gradient methods because their update depends on which policy chose the actions. If the data came from an older or different policy, the gradient is biased unless you correct for it with importance weights. Tree-search methods like AlphaZero and MuZero avoid this. The policy isn't trained on the actions that were taken. It's trained by supervised learning to imitate what the search recommended in each state, using the MCTS visit counts as targets. That target is a better policy than the raw network, and it's still a valid target no matter which policy reached the state.

So old states in the buffer still give a correct learning signal. They also help: they cover more of the state space, make training batches less correlated, and help the network avoid forgetting earlier situations. The main risk is stale targets, especially value targets built from multi-step returns of the old policy. MuZero Reanalyse fixes this by re-running search on old states with the current network to produce fresh targets. That lets it reuse old data many times, which makes learning much more data-efficient.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
In reinforcement learning with tree search (such as AlphaZero or MuZero), training on an off-policy replay buffer often helps because the policy targets are not raw actions from an older network, but improved action distributions produced by lookahead search. Since tree search acts as a policy improvement operator, targets from recent past iterations are frequently still informative and stronger than the raw policy alone.

Replaying past self-play data also breaks strong temporal correlations between consecutive game states, reducing gradient variance and preventing the network from overfitting to a narrow slice of recent games. Equally important, older trajectories preserve a wider distribution of states—including suboptimal lines and mistakes the current policy rarely visits. Training on these diverse positions prevents catastrophic forgetting and keeps the value and policy networks well-calibrated when tree search explores unfamiliar branches. As long as the buffer window is not overly stale (or targets are refreshed via re-search, as in MuZero Reanalyze), these gains in sample efficiency, stability, and generalization outweigh off-policy bias.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
An off-policy replay buffer can help because an old policy may have visited states that are still useful to learn from. The policy can train on what tree search recommends in those states. Search looks ahead and compares possible outcomes, so its recommendations can improve on the actions the older policy actually took. Training on those recommendations teaches the policy to make some of the same decisions without having to search every time.

Replay also lets the learner reuse expensive search results and revisit useful states that the current policy rarely encounters. The benefit depends on how relevant the stored states and targets still are. If old search targets become stale, rerunning search with the current model can refresh them while preserving the value of the stored experience.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
An off-policy replay buffer records states that earlier policies visited. Training on those states can still help because tree search can produce a better action distribution than the policy that collected them. For example, an older policy might choose a weak move, but a fresh search from the same position can identify a stronger one. The policy then learns to favor the stronger move.

Replay also reuses costly experience and keeps rare positions in training after the current policy stops visiting them regularly. The benefit depends on whether the stored states are still relevant and the training targets are reliable. Refreshing stale targets with a new search can help preserve that benefit as the policy improves.
